# Comparison: American Airlines Group vs. Southwest Airlines, FY2024

**Comparability note:** Both companies report on a calendar fiscal year (Jan 1 – Dec 31, 2024), so the periods are directly comparable [DOC: american_southwest_fy2024.txt — "Selected figures from each company's fiscal year 2024 Form 10-K (all calendar-year, Jan 1 - Dec 31)"]. However, they are not comparable in scale or business mix: American is a global network carrier with roughly twice Southwest's revenue ($54,211M vs. $27,483M), while Southwest is a domestic point-to-point carrier. The available excerpts contain only selected income-statement and balance-sheet line items — no cash/liquidity balances, total assets, operating cash flow, lease obligations, or interest expense — so a full leverage and liquidity assessment is not possible from this source.

## Income statement (FY2024)

| Metric | American | Southwest |
|---|---|---|
| Total operating revenue | $54,211M | $27,483M |
| Operating income | $2,614M | $321M |
| Operating margin | 4.8% | 1.2% |
| Net income | $846M | $465M |
| Net margin | 1.6% | 1.7% |

American generated far stronger operating profitability — $2,614M of operating income on a 4.8% margin versus Southwest's $321M on a 1.2% margin [DOC: american_southwest_fy2024.txt — AAL "Operating income: FY2024 $2,614M"; LUV "Operating income: FY2024 $321M"]. But American's much heavier interest burden appears to consume most of that advantage: net income was $846M vs. Southwest's $465M, leaving nearly identical net margins (1.6% vs. 1.7%) [DOC: same].

## Balance sheet (Dec 31, 2024) — the decisive difference

| Metric | American | Southwest |
|---|---|---|
| Total stockholders' equity (deficit) | **–$3,977M** | **+$10,350M** |
| Long-term debt | $24,617M | $6,697M |
| Long-term debt / revenue | 0.45x | 0.24x |

American ended 2024 with a **stockholders' deficit of $3,977M** and $24,617M of long-term debt [DOC: american_southwest_fy2024.txt — AAL "Total stockholders' equity (deficit) at Dec 31: FY2024 -$3,977M. Long-term debt at Dec 31: FY2024 $24,617M"]. Southwest ended with **$10,350M of positive equity** and only $6,697M of long-term debt [DOC: same — LUV "$10,350M... Long-term debt... $6,697M"]. Debt is roughly 3.7x higher at American on revenue only 2.0x larger, and its negative equity means conventional debt-to-equity leverage is undefined/negative.

## Conclusion

The two answers diverge by criterion: **American is the stronger operator** (materially better operating income and margin), but **Southwest is in the stronger financial position** — the question asked. Financial position refers to the balance sheet, and Southwest has positive equity of $10.35B versus American's $3.98B deficit, plus roughly one-quarter of American's long-term debt on half the revenue base. Southwest carries balance-sheet capacity to absorb a demand shock or fund fleet renewal; American is structurally dependent on continued refinancing access, and its thin 1.6% net margin on $54B of revenue leaves little cushion to de-lever.

Caveat: this conclusion rests on equity and long-term debt alone. Liquidity (cash and short-term investments), undrawn revolvers, operating lease liabilities, and near-term maturities are not in the provided excerpts and could shift the margin of the conclusion, though they are very unlikely to reverse a $14.3B equity gap.

ANSWER: Southwest Airlines. On a balance-sheet basis Southwest was clearly stronger at Dec 31, 2024, with +$10,350M of stockholders' equity and $6,697M of long-term debt, versus American's –$3,977M stockholders' deficit and $24,617M of long-term debt. (American was the better operator in FY2024 — $2,614M operating income / 4.8% margin vs. Southwest's $321M / 1.2% — but its interest burden reduced net margins to parity at ~1.6–1.7%, and the two carriers differ materially in scale and business model.)
